sentences.text: Lagenanectes richterae was an elasmosaurid plesiosaur, a marine reptile from the Lower Cretaceous of Lower Saxony, Germany, reaching an estimated length of about 8 meters.

The name means "Leine swimmer," referencing the nearby river and its aquatic life, and the holotype represents a fully grown individual confirmed by the ossification of its cranial bones and vertebrae.
Its lower jaw displays unique features, including sidewards alveols and a platform with prominent dents on the underside.

Private collectors discovered the fossil in 1964 in a clay pit near Sarstedt. Sven Sachs, Jahn J. Hornung, and Benjamin P. Kear formally erected the genus in 2017 after detailed study, naming the species richterae to honor Annette Richter for her paleontological work in the region.
Grooves on the upper side of the skull may have accommodated electroreceptors used to locate prey.
Pathological alterations in the occiput and first neck vertebra may have been caused by an infection.
Research demonstrated that Lagenanectes richterae was an early member of the elasmosaurids.
The fossils are most probably from the upper Hauterivian, though the age might range from the lower Hauterivian to the lower Barremian, placing the animal between 132.6 and 125.77 million years ago.
Cladistic analysis places Lagenanectes in a polytomy with an undescribed plesiosaur from the Speeton Clay and Callawayasaurus.
